faq: John the Ripper (John) is the classic CPU password-hash cracker: feed it a hash file and a wordlist and it reports which passwords match. Auditors use it to prove that weak hashes fall fast — and that slow modern hashes do not.
The tool is legal for audits and recovery. Cracking hashes you do not own or lack permission to test is illegal. Practice on your own lab dumps (DVWA, Metasploitable shadow file).
--wordlist=rockyou.txt tells John to try every line of that file as the password. Most lab passwords fall here because humans reuse common passwords — the single biggest weakness John exploits.
Rules mutate each wordlist entry: add digits, capitalize, append symbols. One base word becomes thousands of guesses, catching real-world patterns like Summer becoming Summer2026!.
--show prints passwords John already cracked from the hash file, so you do not re-crack. Run it first on any file — earlier sessions may have done the work.
How do I crack Linux shadow hashes?
Copy the lab /etc/shadow lines (or unshadow passwd+shadow first), then john --wordlist=rockyou.txt shadow.txt. Lab accounts with weak passwords fall in seconds; strong ones do not.
What is the difference between John and Hashcat?
John runs on CPU and auto-detects many hash formats — easiest start. Hashcat runs on GPU and tries billions per second — fastest finish. Learn the workflow on John, scale to Hashcat.
How do I make my hashes uncrackable?
Store passwords with bcrypt or argon2 (slow, salted), require 12+ random characters via a manager, and add 2FA. Then test with John yourself: an exhausted wordlist with zero cracks is the goal.

issues: Wrong file format: John needs raw hashes, one per line. For shadow files run unshadow passwd shadow first, then crack the output.
The password is not in the wordlist, or the format needs forcing. Try --rules, a bigger list (SecLists), and --format matching the hash type.
That is bcrypt working as designed — slow. In labs crack the fast hashes (MD5, NTLM) and treat bcrypt resistance as the lesson, not a bug.
On Kali: gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz. Pass the full path with --wordlist= on every run.
name: John the Ripper
overview_p1: John the Ripper turns hash files back into passwords: wordlist in, matches out. A DVWA MD5 dump falls in seconds — the visceral proof that fast unsalted hashes protect nothing.
overview_p2: Then flip it: re-hash with bcrypt, require long random passwords, add 2FA — and watch the same tool exhaust its wordlist with zero cracks. That silence is what good password storage sounds like.
overview_sub: Crack lab hashes, then hash right
reqs: Kali Linux (pre-installed) or any OS with CPU
Lab hash files you own (DVWA dump, lab shadow)
Written permission if hashes are not yours

steps.box: Rules catch what plain wordlists miss: the capital letter, the year, the exclamation mark. Real passwords are mutations — rules speak their language.
steps.code:
john --wordlist=short.txt --rules hashes.txt
# Summer2026! cracked via rule
steps.title: Step 2 — Add Rules

steps.box: unshadow merges /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow into John's input format. On Metasploitable the weak accounts fall fast — then you implement the defense below.
steps.code:
unshadow passwd.txt shadow.txt > lab.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt lab.txt
john --show lab.txt
# msfadmin:msfadmin ... cracked
